note_text:
Patient is a 52-year-old woman referred for evaluation of chronic right-sided low back/buttock pain for the past 3 years. She describes non-radiating, unilateral pain localized caudal to L5, directly over the posterior SI joint, worse with prolonged sitting and transitional movements. She has undergone 8 months of conservative management including NSAID and gabapentin optimization, activity/ergonomic modification, and a structured course of active physical therapy focused on core and pelvic stabilization, all with only minimal, transient relief.

On exam, there is focal tenderness to palpation directly over the right posterior SI joint without comparable tenderness at the greater trochanter, lumbar paraspinals, or coccyx. No other obvious pain generator is identified. Provocative testing: thigh thrust test positive on the right, along with positive Gaenslen's and Patrick's (FABER) tests; distraction test negative. Compression test not performed given thigh thrust already positive.

Review of systems and psychiatric history are unremarkable for somatoform disorder or fibromyalgia; no diffuse tender points on exam, pain is well-localized and consistent.

However, further workup for chronicity of symptoms revealed inflammatory markers were checked given morning stiffness lasting >45 minutes and improvement with activity - ESR and CRP were elevated, and HLA-B27 returned positive. Rheumatology consultation confirmed a diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis based on sacroiliitis findings on imaging bilaterally and clinical criteria. Given this systemic inflammatory arthropathy diagnosis, the patient is not an appropriate candidate for percutaneous SIJ fusion despite her localized symptoms and positive provocative maneuvers.

Imaging: Plain radiographs of the pelvis and bilateral hips show no hip osteoarthritis. CT of the SI joints shows bilateral sacroiliitis changes with erosive change consistent with the underlying spondyloarthropathy, without frank tumor or acute infection. Lumbar spine MRI shows mild degenerative disc disease without significant central or foraminal stenosis and no nerve root compression correlating with her symptoms.

The patient underwent two separate image-guided, contrast-enhanced right SI joint injections with local anesthetic, each providing greater than 75% reduction in pain for the expected duration of the anesthetic, confirming the SI joint as the pain source.

Given the confirmed diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis, she is excluded from consideration for percutaneous SIJ fusion; she will be referred back to rheumatology for optimization of systemic therapy.
